key_features.classic_presentation: Kidney stone presents with sudden-onset severe colicky flank pain radiating to groin. Pain comes in waves, patient cannot find comfortable position (writhing in pain). Hematuria (blood in urine) in 85%. Nausea and vomiting common.
key_features.typical_demographics: Peak age 30-50 years. Male predominance (2:1). Higher in hot climates, dehydration, family history. 12% lifetime risk.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Stone passes from kidney into ureter causing obstruction, ureteral spasm, and severe colicky pain.

diagnostic_questions.context: Flank pain is classic. Starts in back/side and radiates anteriorly.
Radiation to groin/genitals is highly specific (stone moving down ureter). Follows ureteral path.
Colicky pattern (waves) due to ureteral peristalsis. Severe during spasms, better between.
Patients with kidney stones are restless/writhing (vs appendicitis where they lie still).
Hematuria in 85%. Dysuria and frequency when stone near bladder.
Onset is typically sudden and dramatic, reaching maximum intensity quickly.
Nausea/vomiting common (50%) due to shared nerve pathways.
Acute onset, typically hours to 1-2 days.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: RLQ pain, migration pattern, patient lies still
Hemodynamic instability, pulsatile mass, older age

red_flags.action: Possible infected stone (pyonephrosis) - urgent care needed
Bilateral obstruction or single kidney - emergency

typical_management: Pain control (NSAIDs, opioids), IV fluids, alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) to facilitate passage. Most stones <5mm pass spontaneously. Larger stones may need lithotripsy or ureteroscopy.
disposition: Emergency department for pain control and imaging. Most can be discharged with urology follow-up. Admission if intractable pain, infection, or obstruction.
patient_education: Kidney stones are mineral crystals that can block the urinary tract. Most pass on their own with hydration and pain medication. Larger stones may need procedures. Increase fluid intake to prevent recurrence.
